sections.history: Tiruvidaiyaru, the village now known as T. Edayar, stands on the southern bank of the Then Pennai river in the old Nadu Nadu country, the stretch of the Tamil land between the Kaveri and the northern Pennar across which the hymns of the Tevaram were sung. The temple of Idaiyattrunathar is counted among the shrines of this region praised by the saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam; the decad sung here is remembered as the work of Sundarar, who set the Lord of Idaiyaru among the sacred Shiva temples of his verses. The Lord is also called Marundeeswarar, a name carrying the sense of the divine physician who heals the ills of body and spirit. The shrine is an old foundation of the Chola country, raised and enlarged in stone by the patrons of the medieval Tamil land and kept in living worship down the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest but ancient Dravidian foundation set among fields near the river. The sanctum of Idaiyattrunathar faces west, an orientation unusual among Shiva shrines and held to be auspicious here. The goddess, honoured as Sittridai Nayaki and in some accounts as Gnanambikai, stands in her own shrine facing east, so that the Lord and his consort look toward one another across the temple, an arrangement devotees hold dear for the blessing of marriage. Within the enclosure grows the sacred marutha tree, the great arjuna beneath which the temple's chief legend unfolds, and the parrots about the grounds are linked by tradition to the sage who did penance here. The full extent of the older structure is not well recorded, and much of what stands reflects the additions of later centuries.
sections.legends: The temple's defining story belongs to the sage Suka, remembered in the tradition as Sukabrahma. Bound by a curse, he is said to have come to Tiruvidaiyaru and performed long penance beneath the marutha tree within the temple, and by the grace of Idaiyattrunathar to have been freed from his burden and granted divine favour. Because the sage's name is also the word for a parrot, the parrots that gather about the temple are held to be his companions, and their presence is cherished as a living sign of the legend. The west-facing Lord and the east-facing goddess, set to behold one another, give the shrine its further repute as a place where obstacles to marriage are loosened, and families come to seek that grace.
sections.festivals: As at every Shiva temple, Maha Shivaratri is the great night of the year, and the monthly Pradosham twilight is kept with devotion. The Tamil festival months of Panguni and Chithirai bring the temple's processions and observances, and the sixty-three Nayanmar saints are honoured in the Shaiva manner. Being a smaller village shrine, its calendar follows local custom and the Tamil almanac, so devotees are advised to confirm the days and the car festival timings with the temple before visiting.
sections.experience: Tiruvidaiyaru rewards the traveller who seeks out the quieter shrines of the Tamil country. The temple sits amid fields near the Then Pennai, away from the bustle of the pilgrim towns, and keeps the still air of an old riverside sanctuary. Come before the west-facing Lord Idaiyattrunathar, honoured as the healer, and then to the goddess in her east-facing shrine; pause beneath the sacred marutha tree where the sage is said to have found release, and watch for the parrots that tradition links to his story. Devotees who carry prayers for health or for marriage hold the place especially dear. The village lies off the Tirukkovilur road, and a short local journey brings the unhurried visitor to its gate.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; as this is a village temple, confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvidaiyaru, now called T. Edayar, lies on the Tirukkovilur–Tiruvennainallur–Arasur road (SH 68), on the southern bank of the Then Pennai river, about 5 km from Tiruvennainallur. Tirukkovilur is the nearest town, and Villupuram, the district centre, is the nearest major railway junction, some distance to the north-east. Local buses from Villupuram and Tirukkovilur serve the village; confirm the route locally, as services to smaller villages can be infrequent.
